title: Students Aren't Engaged, Motivated, or Interested
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey uses the airline industry as a metaphor for understanding student disengagement in higher education. While people tolerate the discomfort of flying because they value the destination, airlines still carefully choreograph the experience to make discomfort psychologically survivable. Higher education dismisses the importance of the learning experience itself, assuming that degree value excuses poor course design. Dempsey applies David Maister's psychology of waiting research to show that students' disengagement stems not from laziness but from educational experiences that are psychologically unintelligible—with unexplained waits, uncertain timelines, and disconnection from purpose.
points: Higher education conflates degree value with ability to disregard course experience design, assuming that degree importance excuses course quality—but this contradicts what the airline industry understands about human psychology. David Maister's research shows that psychological experience is shaped by perception, not just reality: uncertain waits feel longer, unexplained processes feel interminable, and anxious states distort time perception. Students' lack of engagement is not primarily a motivation or discipline problem but a design problem—educational experiences often fail to signal progress, explain purpose, or provide the psychological signals that make discomfort survivable. Airlines maintain discomfort-survivability through choreography: clear phases, small forms of agency, reassurance that each phase will end, and visible progress—elements largely absent from higher education structures. People tolerate difficulty when they understand the value of what they're moving toward and perceive the experience as having psychological coherence and forward momentum.
quotes: Airlines do not make flying comfortable. But they do make discomfort psychologically survivable. That is the whole insight.
The experience of waiting is not determined only by how long people wait. It is shaped by what the wait feels like.
Higher education has spent a very long time defending discomfort while neglecting the conditions that help human beings endure it.
The value of the destination does not remove the need to design the journey.
